Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares their own experience. Respect ceremony traditions. Handle Nate gently; someone in the room may feel like him, and 988 is there any time.

Every student in the room

Some Indigenous communities use psychedelic plants in ceremony with their own traditions, some students have a family history of psychosis or bipolar disorder, and some are struggling with depression; keep all three in mind.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

One thing per card, no names. Read a few aloud and sort them on the board. Expect: cures depression, microdosing helps focus, you can get stuck, it’s natural so it’s safe, gas-station gummies. Come back to “not sure” at the end.

Slide 3 · Notes

Medial prefrontal cortex: the inner narrator quiets. Posterior cingulate: its link weakens and the sense of self can slip. Thalamus: the filter lets more in, less sorted. Visual cortex: patterns and motion that aren’t there. Some find it freeing, others terrifying, and nobody picks in advance. (Carhart-Harris et al., PNAS, 2012)

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain what psilocybin and LSD change in the brain, read psychedelic headlines critically (promising adult trials versus unscreened use), and know what to do for a friend having a hard trip. The tone is curious and evidence-first, avoiding both hype and scare stories.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards for the exit card
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minWhat have you heard? Cards in three piles
  2. 7 minHow it works: the mixing board
  3. 9 minHeadline vs. reality, one per slide
  4. 4 minWhat’s in the bag, and what can go wrong
  5. 5 minSame drug, different trip: turn and talk, share out
  6. 7 minThree situations: Kai, Zoe, Nate
  7. 4 minHard trip steps
  8. 4 minEvery student, exit card

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

What have you heard, the mixing board, the depression headline, Nate, and the hard trip steps.

Before you teach
Run it as media literacy.

The headline vote works because it's about how claims spread. Keep the focus there and off anyone's personal experience.

Give the research its due.

Early adult trials are real and promising. Students who've heard the podcasts will trust you more if you say so before adding the limits.

Watch for students who are struggling.

A student who's felt low for months may see psilocybin as hope. If someone says they plan to treat their own depression, thank them and connect them with a counselor that day. The real research involves screening and therapy.

Family history matters here.

Psychosis, schizophrenia or bipolar disorder in a parent or sibling raises the risk. Mention it as information, and offer the nurse or a counselor to anyone who wants to talk it through privately.

Know the emergency line.

Hurting themselves or someone else, a seizure, chest pain, trouble breathing, or getting very sick after a product: 911 or event medical staff. An emotional crisis without physical danger: 988.

Expect questions about legality.

Psilocybin and LSD are illegal in Massachusetts. In 2024 about 57% of voters rejected legalizing psilocybin and some other natural psychedelics. State it and move on.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Indigenous traditions.

Some Indigenous communities have used psychedelic plants and mushrooms in ceremony for centuries, with guides, rules and preparation. Treat that as its own thing, separate from a party or a store gummy, and never as a joke.

Family mental health history.

Some students know a parent or sibling has bipolar disorder or schizophrenia; some don't know their family history at all, including students who were adopted or are in foster care. Offer "if you don't know, that's worth finding out" gently.

Faith and culture.

For some families any drug talk is off limits; others see natural remedies as safer than medicine. Keep the facts about the brain and leave values to the family.

Access to mental health care.

Students without easy access to therapy may see a mushroom as the only treatment they can reach. Point them to the counselor and free options.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD or anxiety may hear microdosing pitched for focus or calm. The blinded study found real microdoses and empty capsules worked about the same.

Mixed names and situations.

Keep the scenario names and settings varied. Festivals, family gatherings and school weeks all fit.

What the research says

Psilocybin and LSD act mainly on serotonin 2A receptors, which are packed into the cortex.

Nichols, Pharmacological Reviews, 2016

In brain imaging, psilocybin lowered activity in the medial prefrontal cortex and weakened its connection with the posterior cingulate; the bigger the drop, the stronger the trip.

Carhart-Harris et al., PNAS, 2012

59 adults with long-term depression got two psilocybin sessions or six weeks of a standard antidepressant, both with therapy. Psilocybin did about as well and wasn't significantly better on the main measure.

Carhart-Harris et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2021

Research guidelines screen out anyone with a personal or family history of psychosis, use measured doses of pure drug, and keep trained monitors present. Overwhelming distress is the most likely risk.

Johnson, Richards and Griffiths, Journal of Psychopharmacology, 2008

In a self-blinded study, people microdosing with real doses and people taking empty capsules improved about the same over four weeks.

Szigeti et al., eLife, 2021

Poison center calls about psilocybin among 12 to 17 year olds rose 317% between 2019 and 2023.

Rockhill et al., Annals of Internal Medicine, 2025

Diamond Shruumz chocolates and gummies were recalled in 2024 after at least 48 illnesses in 24 states, including seizures, 27 hospitalizations and one possible death.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2024
